A line of best fit runs through a scatterplot so you can predict y from x. The SAT loves to ask what the numbers in that line actually mean.
Here's a model. y equals two point five x plus forty, where x is hours studied and y is a test score.
The slope is two point five. Slope is a rate, like miles per hour. For each one more hour of studying, the predicted score goes up two point five points.
The intercept is forty. It's the predicted y when x is zero. So a student who studies zero hours is predicted to score forty.
Trap alert. Don't swap them. The slope is the rate of change. The intercept is the starting value, when x is zero.
Now predict. For six hours, plug in six. Two point five times six is fifteen. Add forty, and the prediction is fifty five.
If you said fifteen, you forgot the intercept. Always add the b.
A residual is actual minus predicted. Points above the line have positive residuals. Points below the line have negative residuals.
A student studied six hours and actually scored sixty. Predicted was fifty five. Sixty minus fifty five is a residual of five.
Trap alert. Predicted minus actual gives negative five. That's backwards. It's always actual minus predicted.

Now try x equals three. Three cubed is twenty seven, but four times three plus one is thirteen. The exponential eventually passes the linear one, but not always.
